{{short description|American theoretical physicist}}
{{BLP sources|date=August 2018}}
'''David Joseph Singh''' (born 1958) is a theoretical [[physicist]] who is a curators' professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the [[University of Missouri]] in Columbia, Missouri.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://faculty.missouri.edu/singhdj/|title=Home - David J. Singh, Condensed Matter and Materials Theory, University of Missouri|website=faculty.missouri.edu|access-date=2017-10-12|archive-date=2018-12-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181202150159/http://faculty.missouri.edu/singhdj/|url-status=dead}}</ref> He was previously a corporate fellow at the [[Oak Ridge National Laboratory]] (ORNL).

== Early life and education ==

David Joseph Singh was born in [[Cedar Rapids, Iowa]] on June 23, 1958, and attended high school at [[Ashbury College]] in Ottawa, Canada. He obtained a ''[[summa cum laude]]'' [[B.Sc.]] (1980) and a [[Ph.D.]] (1985) in [[physics]] from the [[University of Ottawa]] in Canada. From 1985 to 1988, Singh had a [[postdoctoral appointment]] at the [[College of William and Mary]]. In 1988, Singh moved to join the theory group at the [[Naval Research Laboratory]] in [[Washington, D.C.]] From 1988 to 2004, he continued to work on a range of materials problems, including [[colossal magnetoresistance]], at the Naval Research Laboratory.<ref>Warren E. Pickett et al, Phys. Rev. B.53,1146 (1996).</ref>

In 2004, Singh left Washington to join the [[Oak Ridge National Laboratory]], a [[United States Department of Energy]] facility, in [[Oak Ridge, Tennessee]]. In 2015, he moved to the [[University of Missouri]].<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://munews.missouri.edu/news-releases/2016/0505-internationally-recognized-physics-researcher-joins-faculty/ |title = MU News Bureau &#124; MU News Bureau}}</ref>

== Career ==

Singh co-authored ''Planewaves, Pseudopotentials and the LAPW Method'' and approximately 500 publications in scientific journals. His general area of research is in [[condensed matter physics]] with a focus on [[electronic structure]] methods, [[ferroelectrics]], [[thermoelectrics]]<ref>O. Delaire et al, Nature Materials, 10, 614 (2011).</ref><ref>G. Xing et al., Physical Review Materials 1, 065405 (2017) https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevMaterials.1.065405</ref> and [[iron-based superconductor]]s.<ref>M.M. Quazilbash et al, Nature Physics.5,647 (2009).</ref> He has contributed to the application of [[density functional theory]], especially to iron-based superconductors,<ref>Michelle D. Johannes, Viewpoint: The iron age of superconductivity, https://physics.aps.org/articles/v1/28</ref> and methods.<ref>Y. Fu, et al. Physical Review Letters 121, 207201 (2018) https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.121.207201</ref>

Along with his former colleague and a frequent collaborator Igor I. Mazin, Singh developed the sign-changing [[s-wave]] model for [[iron-based superconductors]].<ref>I.I. Mazin et al, Phys. Rev. Lett.101,057003 (2008).</ref>

== Memberships and awards ==

Singh became a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] in 1997.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=S&|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=www.aps.org}}</ref> He was an editorial board member of the ''[[New Journal of Physics]]''<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://iopscience.iop.org/journal/1367-2630/page/Editorial%20Board%20Members |title = Editorial Board - New Journal of Physics - IOPscience}}</ref> and ''[[Scientific Reports]]''. He is also a Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry.

Singh was a corporate fellow at [[Oak Ridge National Laboratory]].<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.ornl.gov/our-people/corporate-fellows |title = Corporate Fellows &#124; ORNL}}</ref> He received the E.O. Hulburt Annual Science Award and the Gordon Battelle Prize.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ornl.gov/news/five-ornl-scientists-rated-among-worlds-most-influential|title=Five ORNL scientists rated among world's most influential - ORNL|website=www.ornl.gov}}</ref>
